lines.n: And then, just as I was sure I would give in, the cold slid off into the brush, leaving a trail of shrinking plants behind it. Lucien let out his breath. The horses shook their heads. Even the crocuses seemed to straighten.

lines.t: No. It was a thing that shouldn't be in these lands at all. We call it the Bogge. You can't hunt it, and you can't kill it. Not even with your precious ash arrows.
Because once you look at it, once you admit it's there, it becomes real. And then it can kill you.
It spoke to me. In my head. It kept telling me to look.
Well, thank the Cauldron you didn't. Scraping you off the path would have ruined the rest of my day.

lines.n: We rode for an hour without much talk. When I'd stopped shaking, I couldn't help myself.

lines.t: You're old, you carry a sword and you ride patrol. Did you fight in the War?
Cauldron, Feyre, I'm not that old.
Not as good as Tam. But I know which end of a blade to hold. Shall I teach you, mighty mortal huntress? Or do you only need to know where to aim?
I've never held a sword. Hunting's all I know.
I suppose you'd have wet yourself and curled up to die, if you'd known what Andras really was. Do you ever stop being so serious? So dull?

lines.n: I bit my tongue. He sighed, bored, and needled me again about the squirrels, and the weather, and my seat on the horse, until I couldn't stand it.

lines.t: Do you ever stop being such a prick?

lines.n: I should have been dead for that. Truly, I should. But Lucien only grinned at me.
Alis, it seemed, had not been wrong.
Tamlin was sprawled in his chair, one long claw circling the rim of his goblet. It stopped dead when I walked in. I'd turned down his ride this morning, saying I wanted to be alone.

lines.t: So I heard. Did you enjoy yourselves?

lines.n: Lucien left the answer to me. Coward.
He looked at me for a long moment, then turned to his food. Lucien cleared his throat.

lines.t: Tam. The Bogge was in the woods today.

lines.n: Tamlin's fork bent double in his fist.

lines.t: It passed us. Close. It must have slipped over the border.

lines.n: Metal shrieked as his claws punched out and shredded what was left of the fork. He rose, and his teeth seemed longer than before.
Lucien told him. Tamlin threw one look at me and stalked out, and shut the door behind him with terrible gentleness.

lines.t: You said it couldn't be killed. That you couldn't even face it.

lines.n: The male who'd served me with his own hands that first night could kill a thing like that. I didn't know what to do with the thought. It wasn't my problem.
And just because Lucien had stopped eating didn't mean I had to. He never noticed the feast I put away.
With nothing else to do, I sharpened my stolen knife on a stone from the garden and kept an eye on the lawn below my window.
An hour went by. He didn't come back. I told myself I didn't care whether he survived it.
The moon came up, silvering the garden. Ridiculous, to be waiting up for him. I turned to go to bed.
Something moved below. Not Tamlin. Someone standing by the hedges, facing the house. Looking up at me.
A man, hunched over a cane. He limped two steps into the light from the house.
My father had come. My broken, crippled father had come all this way to take me home.
I didn't let myself think. I pulled on tunic over tunic, bundled into a cloak, stuffed the stolen knife into my boot, and climbed out of the window onto the wisteria.
